paragraphs: Sixteen-bit math is one of the cheapest speedups in deep learning, and one of the quietest ways to break a run. Some updates round away to nothing. Some values turn into infinity. Often, nothing logs an error.

It comes down to two limits every float has: how big a number it can hold, and how close together two numbers can sit. FP16 and BF16 bet differently on those, so each fails in its own place, and the fix depends on which number is in trouble.

You'll look at a weight's actual neighbors, rescue a tiny gradient with loss scaling, watch a controller skip a bad step, and build a memory budget that shows why mixed precision doesn't halve your memory.
Keep the last chapter's training run in mind, since all of this changes how its updates land. The small examples run on any laptop. Speed and quality still have to be measured on your own hardware.
outcomes: Tell apart overflow, underflow, and an update lost to rounding.
Put scaling, unscaling, clipping, and accumulation in the right order.
Budget memory by component and choose a precision with a controlled comparison.
question: Where in your training run could learning disappear while every number stays finite?
